answer:
So we’ve taken a look at many SaaS leaders over the years on our New New Podcast and Live Wednesday series.  But one I think we haven’t done enough is Atlassian.  Because they’re so interesting.  They started off as a developer tool and got pretty big (and then even bigger).  It took them a while to really go enterprise, but when they did … wow.
$2.7 billion in ARR
Growing 21%, with
37% Subscription Growth
That’s just incredible efficiency for an enterprise play!
25% Free Cash Flow Margins (!)
And importantly — it gets better:
100% NRR
Not bad for a product that doesn’t have sales reps!  More on this below
110% GRR / Net Retention Rate
A related metric, but higher than NRR because it includes upsells, etc.  And again, without traditional sales support.  Wow.
Incredibly Efficient Hiring
Only 230 employees to serve 300,000 customers!  A stunning ratio.
What’s more impressive?  This was all during Covid.
Let’s take a look at some learnings:

#1.  60% of its Business Customers Are Outside Tech
While half their users are techies, 60% of their customers outside tech, and 40% of those are “non-technical” departments like HR and finance.  So don’t worry too much if your early leads aren’t technically savvy.  Just make sure you can get them into production quickly.  And keep the product simple enough to deploy there.
#2.  100% NRR, With 50% of Revenue From Self-Serve + Freemium Editions
Atlassian does have sales, but a lot less than most of us.  Most of its top partners are solution providers.  That means Atlassian has gotten almost 100% NRR out of self-service and freemium editions alone!  That’s what it takes to scale efficiently.

So Atlassian has cruised past $4 Billion in ARR, still growing a steady 21% in a very efficient fashion.  It’s raining cash, with 27% free-cash flow margins.
The markets like this combination.  Even with a few bumps, Atlassian is still trading at a $55 Billion market cap, so over 12x ARR.  That’s twice the average of 6x ARR for public SaaS companies.
Efficient, steady, profitable growth at scale.  The markets say Yes to Atlassian.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  300,000 Total Paying Customers, With 43,000 Paying $10k or More
The vast majority of Atlassian’s customers pay less than $10k a year, but the $10k+ ones make up the bulk of the revenue.  A reminder that the long tail really does work in collaboration.  And also how important it is to go a smidge upmarket if you sell to SMBs and smaller customers.

So Atlassian is bucking the trend. At almost $5B ARR, subscription growth is up a stunning 33%, and revenue overall up 21% The markets loved it, driving the stock up +29% the past month Is SaaS Back? 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. Raising Guidance and Growth Rate for Cloud Revenue That’s pretty darn impressive growth at almost $5B in ARR, and just as importantly, they’re raising their prediction here. Atlassian is bullish on maintain and accelerating Cloud growth over the next year. #2. 500 $1M+ Customers Atlassian is going more and more enterprise, which has become key to maintaining growth. It now has 500 $1M+ customers. #3. 51% of Revenue From Outside North America A reminder to go global as early as practical. #4. 50% of Users on "Business Side”, 50% Technical An interesting breakdown across their core products. Yes, Atlassian’s roots are selling to developers. But as you go more upmarket, and more enterprise, the business users become critical stakeholders and users, too. It’s split 50/50 at Atlassian. #5. Seat Expansion Driving Growth, Along with Cross-Sell of New Products Long live per-seat models and pricing! Atlassian, HubSpot, GitLab and more are seeing growth fueled by classic account expansion of more seats. _______ The Atlassian engine just keeps on running!! Even at almost $5 Billion in ARR. Pretty impressive. Pretty, pretty impressive.

#5.  Planning to Hit $10B ARR in 5 Years
The beauty of recurring revenue and 100%+ NRR — that is, if you are also growing net new customer count too.  Which is Atlassian is.  You can predict long-term growth with fairly high confidence.
And a few other interesting learnings:

#6.  Continuing to See Pressures on Seat Counts — And Plan to Continue to Increase Prices
Atlassian isn’t immune from customers’ desires to cut and minimize seat count.  It just hasn’t seen the dramatic impact there
Salesforce
and others have.   They also plan to offset this with more price increases.
#7.  12,000 Employees, So About $370,000 in Revenue Per Employee
You don’t need to be here in the start-up phase.  But the leaders in SaaS and Cloud all seem to be
skating toward $400k in revenue per employee
to hit Wall Street’s profitability expectations.
Pretty cool, Atlassian.  Pretty cool.

They did that, and that took them through almost $100 million in revenue, which then led to an IPO. The IPO came, and what happened? Well, the market was tough after Covid. So Atlassian has cruised past $4 Billion in ARR, still growing a steady 21% in a very efficient fashion.  It’s raining cash, with 27% free-cash flow margins.
The markets like this combination.  Even with a few bumps, Atlassian is still trading at a $55 Billion market cap, so over 12x ARR.  That’s twice the average of 6x ARR for public SaaS companies.
Efficient, steady, profitable growth at scale.  The markets say Yes to Atlassian.
5 Interesting Learnings:
#1.  300,000 Total Paying Customers, With 43,000 Paying $10k or More
The vast majority of Atlassian’s customers pay less than $10k a year, but the $10k+ ones make up the bulk of the revenue.  A reminder that the long tail really does work in collaboration.  And also how important it is to go a smidge upmarket if you sell to SMBs and smaller customers.

So Atlassian is bucking the trend. At almost $5B ARR, subscription growth is up a stunning 33%, and revenue overall up 21% The markets loved it, driving the stock up +29% the past month Is SaaS Back? 5 Interesting Learnings: #1. Raising Guidance and Growth Rate for Cloud Revenue That’s pretty darn impressive growth at almost $5B in ARR, and just as importantly, they’re raising their prediction here. Atlassian is bullish on maintain and accelerating Cloud growth over the next year. #2. 500 $1M+ Customers Atlassian is going more and more enterprise, which has become key to maintaining growth. It now has 500 $1M+ customers. #3. 51% of Revenue From Outside North America A reminder to go global as early as practical. #4. 50% of Users on "Business Side”, 50% Technical An interesting breakdown across their core products. Yes, Atlassian’s roots are selling to developers. But as you go more upmarket, and more enterprise, the business users become critical stakeholders and users, too. It’s split 50/50 at Atlassian. #5. Seat Expansion Driving Growth, Along with Cross-Sell of New Products Long live per-seat models and pricing! Atlassian, HubSpot, GitLab and more are seeing growth fueled by classic account expansion of more seats. _______ The Atlassian engine just keeps on running!! Even at almost $5 Billion in ARR. Pretty impressive. Pretty, pretty impressive.

#5.  Planning to Hit $10B ARR in 5 Years
The beauty of recurring revenue and 100%+ NRR — that is, if you are also growing net new customer count too.  Which is Atlassian is.  You can predict long-term growth with fairly high confidence.
And a few other interesting learnings:

#6.  Continuing to See Pressures on Seat Counts — And Plan to Continue to Increase Prices
Atlassian isn’t immune from customers’ desires to cut and minimize seat count.  It just hasn’t seen the dramatic impact there
Salesforce
and others have.   They also plan to offset this with more price increases.
#7.  12,000 Employees, So About $370,000 in Revenue Per Employee
You don’t need to be here in the start-up phase.  But the leaders in SaaS and Cloud all seem to be
skating toward $400k in revenue per employee
to hit Wall Street’s profitability expectations.
Pretty cool, Atlassian.  Pretty cool.

“Customers won’t trust an AI.”
And often, the next part is “especially if something goes wrong.  They’ll just blame us.”

I asked our team — which included two of our best salespeople who’d never worked with AI before —

The reasons were simple:
availability
— our AI reps could work 24/7, answer questions instantly
knowledge depth
— our AI knew everything about SaaStr’s products cold, no research needed
no BS or lies
— unlike some human reps, our AI didn’t make stuff up to close deals

Here’s where we’re actually at right now, based entirely on real data and usage patterns:

answer: So I was chatting with someone at another company recently. They were excited about their new AI VP of Sales — which sounds awesome, except that AI VPs aren’t really ready to sell yet. And the thing just made stuff up. No problem. That’s why I wasn’t going to buy anything from them. You probably had a similar experience as a buyer too. Now look, this is important. We all say things sometimes that aren’t true. We stretch data points. We exaggerate a bit. These things happen. But an AI system has no idea if it’s giving you correct information or not. Or worse, maybe it gives you mostly right info, then says something wrong. That just totally destroys credibility. When we’re shopping online now, we expect the same level of transparency and truthfulness from digital systems as we demand from people. If a website makes a claim that turns out to be false, you lose our trust immediately. And honestly, we also expect more from AI than from a lot of salespeople these days. The bar is higher. Don’t let your team pretend otherwise. But here’s my point: AI can already process and synthesize vast amounts of data in real-time, faster and more accurately than any human.
